newsitem.title: CHINA: Shares rebound after Deng shock but fears remain.
newsitem.headline: Shares rebound after Deng shock but fears remain.

text.p: Rumour and speculation over the health of China's paramount leader Deng Xiaoping flowed on unchecked on Wednesday but there was a steadying of east Asian share prices hard hit this week by fears for his life.

A Chinese source and Western diplomats said China's communist leadership had dissolved Deng's once-powerful personal office, in what could be a sign that the health of the 92-year-old patriarch was increasingly fragile

Stock markets in Hong Kong, Taiwan and China closed higher as Deng-related worries that had sent them slumping on Tuesday began to dissipate, but Beijing officials made no further effort to calm fears that the aged reformer's end could be near.

Deng has not been seen in public since the 1994 Chinese Lunar New Year festival, when he appeared frail and faltering, and a Chinese source said his office of advisers and secretaries was dissolved shortly before the Lunar New Year on February 7.
"If true, it is a signal Deng's health had deteriorated... Deng can no longer sustain a very active role in the political sphere," said a Western diplomat who had heard about the move.
The dissolution of the Deng office also signalled China's succession problem was virtually resolved and that President Jiang had consolidated his position as heir apparent.
"Jiang Zemin is eager to tell the world that he is now in charge... and he no longer needs to take directives from Deng's office," said the Chinese source, who has close ties to the Communist Party.
"Deng Xiaoping has been retired for many years... Deng's office has no direct function," the source said.
Deng, whose pragmatic policies transformed a backward Stalinist state into an economic powerhouse, retired from his last official position in 1990.

Chinese sources told Reuters earlier this week that Communist Party chief and state President Jiang Zemin and Premier Li Peng both cut short out-of-town trips last weekend to return to Beijing to visit the ailing patriarch.

A Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman on Tuesday played down worries that Deng's health was deteriorating -- saying there had been "no big change" in his condition, but declining to say what would be considered a major change.
The statement did little to stem the flow of reports, rumours and speculation about Deng's medical prognosis that has swirled around the Chinese capital in recent days.
The Japanese daily Nihon Keizai Shimbun, quoting diplomatic sources in Beijing with close ties to senior military officials, said Deng was critically ill after a brain haemorrhage.
The Chinese leadership had told senior party and government officials not to leave the country unless obliged to do so for pressing diplomatic reasons, the newspaper said.

Japan's Kyodo news agency said Deng suffered a brain haemorrhage last Friday, while Hong Kong's Ming Pao newspaper said the senior leader was recuperating at home from such a haemorrhage but "was not about to die soon".
Officials of Beijing's island arch-rival Taiwan, who have been watching closely for changes in Deng's condition, said they had received no fresh information on the state of his health.
"There has been no change," Defence Minister Chiang Chung-ling said, but gave no details.
Rumours about Deng's health surface periodically and often have a direct impact on China-related bourses, where Deng's demise is seen by some as a potentially destabilising factor.

"Old Deng's health is still the top political concern on the Chinese stock markets," said an executive with one major Chinese brokerage. "The markets will continue to fluctuate sharply in the lead-up to his inevitable death."
Concerns about Deng's health dampened sentiment for a second day in Hong Kong on Wednesday, where the Hang Seng index ended up just 3.38 points or 0.03 percent at 13,106.32.
After falling sharply on Monday and Tuesday, stocks in China's two markets, Shanghai and Shenzhen, moved higher.
Traders said the modest recovery had been prompted by the remarks from Beijing's Foreign Ministry, but said concerns remained and the room for further rises could be limited.
